lessons.title: Sessions and cookies: flags, CSRF and session fixation
lessons.summary: Server-side sessions done properly: random ids, HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite and __Host- cookies, timeouts, layered CSRF defences and regenerating ids to stop fixation.
lessons.body:
## The core idea

HTTP is stateless, so after a user proves who they are, the server needs a way to recognise their next request. A **server-side session** does that with an opaque, random **session id**: the server stores the real state (user id, roles, CSRF secret, created-at, last-seen) in a database or cache, and the browser only holds the id in a cookie. Every request carries the cookie, the server looks the id up, and either finds a live session or treats the caller as anonymous.

The security of the whole scheme rests on three things: the id is unguessable, the cookie cannot be stolen or misused by other sites, and the id changes whenever the trust level changes. Cookie flags (`HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite`, prefixes), CSRF defences and session-fixation protection are just those three ideas made concrete.

Sessions are not old-fashioned. For a first-party web app (your frontend and API on the same site), a server session in an `HttpOnly` cookie is still the default recommendation in the OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet and in most "backend for frontend" designs, because it gives you instant revocation and keeps tokens out of JavaScript.

## How it works, step by step

```text
1. POST /login  {email, password}
2. server verifies password, creates session row:
      id = base64url(32 random bytes)   user=42  created=t0  lastSeen=t0  csrf=...
3. response: Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=<id>; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=1209600
4. browser stores cookie, sends it on matching requests:
      GET /api/me   Cookie: __Host-sid=<id>
5. server: lookup(id) -> check idle + absolute timeout -> load user -> handle request
6. POST /logout -> delete session row -> Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=; Max-Age=0
```

**Session id generation.** Use a CSPRNG (`crypto.randomBytes` in Node, `secrets.token_urlsafe` in Python). OWASP asks for at least 64 bits of entropy; 128-256 bits costs nothing. Never derive ids from user ids, timestamps or counters. A good extra step is to store only a hash (SHA-256) of the id in the database: if the sessions table leaks, the attacker cannot replay the ids.

**Timeouts.** Keep two clocks per session: an **idle timeout** (for example 30 minutes for a bank, days for a consumer app) and an **absolute timeout** (for example 12 hours to 30 days) after which the user must log in again regardless of activity. Update `lastSeen` lazily (say at most once a minute) to avoid a write on every request.

**Storage.** A Postgres or MongoDB table works fine for most apps, with an index on the id and a TTL or cleanup job. Redis is common when you want fast lookups and automatic expiry. Keep a `userId` index so "log out everywhere" and "list my devices" are one query.

## Cookie flags that matter

| Attribute | What it does | Why you want it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `HttpOnly` | JavaScript cannot read the cookie via `document.cookie` | An XSS bug cannot exfiltrate the session id (it can still make requests as the user while the page is open) |
| `Secure` | Sent only over HTTPS | Stops leaks over plain HTTP, including on hostile Wi-Fi |
| `SameSite=Lax` | Not sent on cross-site subrequests (images, fetch, iframes, cross-site POST); sent on top-level GET navigations | Strong default CSRF protection while links from email still log you in |
| `SameSite=Strict` | Never sent on any cross-site request, even a top-level link | Best for high-value actions; users arriving from another site appear logged out on the first page |
| `SameSite=None` | Sent everywhere; requires `Secure` | Only for genuinely cross-site embeds or third-party widgets |
| `Path`, `Domain` | Scope of the cookie | Omit `Domain` so the cookie is host-only and not shared with every subdomain |
| `Max-Age` / `Expires` | Persistence | Without them it is a session cookie that dies with the browser (browsers that restore sessions may keep it) |

**Cookie prefixes** are enforced by the browser. A cookie named `__Host-sid` is only accepted if it has `Secure`, `Path=/` and no `Domain`, which means a compromised or malicious subdomain cannot set or overwrite it. `__Secure-` only requires `Secure`. Use `__Host-` for session cookies whenever you can.

Two details people get wrong. First, **site is not origin**. SameSite compares the *registrable domain* (eTLD+1, for example `example.com`) plus scheme, so `evil.example.com` is same-site with `app.example.com`. SameSite does nothing against a hostile sibling subdomain; host-only `__Host-` cookies and CSRF tokens do. Second, Chrome has treated cookies without a `SameSite` attribute as `Lax` since 2020, but other contexts differ, so always set it explicitly. web.dev's "SameSite cookies explained" walks through the matrix.

## CSRF: what it is and how to stop it

Cross-site request forgery works because the browser attaches cookies automatically. If `bank.com` accepts `POST /transfer` with only a cookie for authentication, a page on `evil.com` can auto-submit a hidden form to it and the browser will include the victim's session cookie.

```text
victim logged in to bank.com
victim visits evil.com  ->  <form action="https://bank.com/transfer" method=POST> auto-submits
browser sends Cookie: sid=...   ->  bank.com sees a valid session and moves money
```

The OWASP CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet recommends layering defences:

1. **SameSite=Lax or Strict** on the session cookie. This blocks the classic cross-site POST. It is defence in depth, not the whole answer: same-site subdomains, old browsers and state-changing GET endpoints still get through.
2. **Never change state on GET.** Lax still sends cookies on top-level GET navigations, so `GET /delete?id=5` is forgeable with a plain link.
3. **Synchronizer token.** Store a random token in the session, render it into forms or expose it via an endpoint, and require it in a header or body field on every unsafe method. Compare in constant time.
4. **Signed double-submit cookie** when you have no server state: put an HMAC of (session id + random value) in a non-HttpOnly cookie and require the same value in a header. The naive unsigned version is weak because an attacker who can write cookies (via a subdomain) can set both.
5. **Fetch metadata and Origin checks.** Modern browsers send `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin | same-site | cross-site | none`. Rejecting unsafe methods when it is `cross-site` is cheap and very effective. Fall back to checking `Origin` against an allowlist.
6. **Custom header requirement** for JSON APIs: a cross-site form cannot set `X-Requested-With` or `Content-Type: application/json` without triggering a CORS preflight, which your server will refuse.

A small Express-style middleware that combines fetch metadata and a token:

```ts
import { timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto";
import type { Request, Response, NextFunction } from "express";

const UNSAFE = new Set(["POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE"]);
const ALLOWED_ORIGINS = new Set(["https://app.example.com"]);

export function csrfGuard(req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) {
  if (!UNSAFE.has(req.method)) return next();

  const site = req.get("sec-fetch-site");
  if (site === "cross-site") return res.status(403).send("cross-site request blocked");

  const origin = req.get("origin");
  if (origin && !ALLOWED_ORIGINS.has(origin)) return res.status(403).send("bad origin");

  const sent = Buffer.from(req.get("x-csrf-token") ?? "");
  const expected = Buffer.from(req.session.csrfToken);
  if (sent.length !== expected.length || !timingSafeEqual(sent, expected)) {
    return res.status(403).send("bad csrf token");
  }
  next();
}
```

Note what CSRF defences do not cover: if the attacker has XSS on your origin, they can read the token and send same-origin requests. CSRF protection assumes your own origin is clean.

## Session fixation

In a fixation attack the attacker gets the victim to use a session id the attacker already knows (planted via a URL parameter on old stacks, a cookie set from a sibling subdomain, or a shared kiosk). When the victim logs in, the server upgrades that same session to authenticated, and the attacker now holds a logged-in id.

The fix is simple and non-negotiable: **issue a brand-new session id whenever the privilege level changes**: login, logout, MFA step-up, role change, password change. Copy over anything you need (cart contents), delete the old row, set the new cookie.

```ts
// express-session
req.session.regenerate((err) => {
  if (err) return next(err);
  req.session.userId = user.id;
  req.session.authAt = Date.now();
  req.session.save(() => res.redirect("/dashboard"));
});
```

Also never accept session ids from URLs, and reject ids your server did not issue (some frameworks will happily create a session with whatever id the client sends).

## Trade-offs and when not to use server sessions

- **Pros:** instant revocation (delete the row), small cookie, no secrets in JavaScript, easy "active devices" UI, server can change roles without waiting for tokens to expire.
- **Cons:** a lookup per request (cheap with an index or Redis; cache the user for a few seconds if needed), a shared store across instances, and cookies are awkward for non-browser clients and truly cross-site APIs.
- **Use tokens instead (or as well)** for third-party API consumers, mobile apps calling many services, and service-to-service calls. Many systems combine both: the browser talks to a backend-for-frontend with a session cookie, and the BFF holds OAuth access tokens server-side.

## Common mistakes and debugging

- Session cookie without `HttpOnly` "because the SPA needs to know if it's logged in". Expose a `/api/me` endpoint instead.
- Setting `Domain=.example.com` so every subdomain, including a marketing site run by a vendor, receives the session.
- `SameSite=None` added to "fix" a login loop without understanding the cross-site flow. Usually the real issue is that the frontend and API are on different sites.
- Not regenerating the id on login (fixation) or not deleting the server row on logout (the cookie is gone, but a stolen copy still works).
- Comparing CSRF tokens with `===` (timing leak, minor) or not at all on JSON endpoints "because it's an API".
- Debugging: in DevTools, Application tab, inspect cookies and look for the yellow warning icon that explains why a cookie was blocked. The Network tab shows `Set-Cookie` rejections per request. Check `Sec-Fetch-Site` on the failing request.

## In the interview

**What they probe:** whether you can explain why cookies plus sessions are secure (and where they are not), the exact effect of each flag, the CSRF threat model, and fixation. Senior interviews push on cross-site deployments, subdomains and revocation.

**A 60-second answer outline:**
1. After login, generate a 128-bit-plus random id, store session state server-side, send the id in a `__Host-` cookie with `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax`.
2. Idle and absolute timeouts; regenerate the id on every privilege change to stop fixation; delete the row on logout.
3. CSRF: SameSite as a baseline, no state change on GET, plus a synchronizer token or fetch-metadata check on unsafe methods.
4. Trade-off versus JWTs: one lookup per request in exchange for instant revocation and no tokens in JavaScript.

**Follow-ups to expect:** "Does SameSite make CSRF tokens unnecessary?" (no: same-site subdomains, GET handlers, older clients); "What does HttpOnly not protect against?" (XSS can still act as the user); "Your frontend is on `app.com` and API on `api.io`, what changes?" (cookies are now cross-site; prefer putting the API behind the same site or a BFF); "How do you implement log out of all devices?"
keyPoints: A session id must be CSPRNG-generated (128+ bits), stored hashed if possible, and carry no meaning on its own.
Use a __Host- cookie with Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax; omit Domain so subdomains never receive it.
SameSite compares sites (eTLD+1), not origins, so it does not protect against a hostile sibling subdomain.
Layer CSRF defences: SameSite, no state change on GET, plus a synchronizer token or Sec-Fetch-Site/Origin check.
Regenerate the session id on login, logout, MFA step-up and role change to stop session fixation.
interview: How do server-side sessions work, and what cookie flags would you set on a session cookie?
What is CSRF, and does SameSite=Lax make CSRF tokens unnecessary?
What is session fixation and how do you prevent it?

check.q: Your app runs on app.example.com and a vendor runs blog.example.com. Which setting stops the blog from reading or overwriting your session cookie?
options: A __Host- prefixed cookie with no Domain attribute
check.why: A __Host- cookie must be host-only (no Domain), Secure and Path=/, so a sibling subdomain can neither receive nor overwrite it. SameSite does not help because both hosts are the same site.

check.q: With the session cookie set to SameSite=Lax, which request from evil.com still carries the cookie?
options: A top-level link navigation to GET /account/delete?id=5
check.why: Lax sends cookies on top-level GET navigations, which is why state must never change on GET. Subresource requests and cross-site POSTs do not get the cookie.

check.q: What is the essential fix for session fixation?
options: Issue a new session id whenever the user's privilege level changes, such as at login
check.why: Fixation relies on the pre-login id surviving authentication. Regenerating the id at login (and other privilege changes) makes the planted id worthless.

lessons.title: JWTs: structure, validation pitfalls, refresh rotation and revocation
lessons.summary: How JWTs are built and signed, the exact validation checklist (and the attacks when you skip it), short-lived access plus rotating refresh tokens, and honest revocation options.
lessons.body:
## The core idea

A **JSON Web Token** is a compact, URL-safe string that carries signed claims, for example "subject 42, issued by auth.example.com, for audience api.example.com, valid until 10:15". Anyone who holds the issuer's verification key can check the signature and trust the claims **without calling the issuer**. That is the whole selling point: stateless verification across many services.

The cost is the mirror image. Because nobody calls the issuer, a valid token stays valid until it expires, even if the user logged out, was fired or had the token stolen. Every JWT design is a negotiation between that statelessness and the need to revoke. The second cost is that JWT libraries and specs have a long history of footguns (`alg: none`, algorithm confusion, unchecked audience) that turn "signed" into "trusted input from the attacker".

Keep one distinction straight: a JWT is a *format*. "Access token", "ID token" and "refresh token" are *roles* in a protocol such as OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect. Access tokens are often JWTs, ID tokens always are, and refresh tokens are usually opaque random strings.

## Structure

A signed JWT (a JWS in compact form, RFC 7515) is three base64url segments joined by dots:

```text
eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6IjIwMjYtMDkifQ . eyJpc3MiOiJodHRwczovL2F1dGguZXhhbXBsZS5jb20iLC4uLn0 . <signature>
        header (JSON)                                 payload / claims (JSON)                          sig over "header.payload"

header:  { "alg": "RS256", "kid": "2026-09", "typ": "at+jwt" }
payload: { "iss": "https://auth.example.com", "sub": "user_42", "aud": "https://api.example.com",
           "exp": 1790000900, "iat": 1790000000, "nbf": 1790000000, "jti": "b1f3...", "scope": "orders:read" }
```

The payload is **encoded, not encrypted**. Anyone can base64-decode it, so never put secrets or personal data you would not show the user in it. If you need confidentiality, JWE (RFC 7516) exists, but most systems simply keep sensitive data out of the token.

Registered claims from RFC 7519: `iss` (issuer), `sub` (subject), `aud` (audience), `exp` (expiry), `nbf` (not before), `iat` (issued at), `jti` (unique id). RFC 9068 defines a profile for JWT access tokens with `typ: at+jwt`, which helps prevent an ID token being accepted as an access token.

## Signing algorithms

| alg | Type | Key | Use when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `HS256` | HMAC-SHA256 | One shared secret | The issuer and verifier are the same service or tightly trusted; every verifier can also mint tokens |
| `RS256` | RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 + SHA-256 | Private key signs, public key verifies | Many verifiers; widely supported default |
| `PS256` | RSA-PSS | Same as above | Preferred RSA padding where supported |
| `ES256` | ECDSA P-256 | Small keys and signatures | Smaller tokens; needs a good RNG per signature (library handles it) |
| `EdDSA` | Ed25519 | Small, fast, deterministic | Good modern choice if all your libraries support it |

The key point with asymmetric algorithms: only the issuer holds the private key, and verifiers fetch public keys from a **JWKS endpoint** (`/.well-known/jwks.json`). The `kid` header tells the verifier which key to use, which is what makes key rotation possible: publish the new key, start signing with it, keep the old key in the JWKS until all tokens it signed have expired, then remove it.

## Validation, and the pitfalls

RFC 8725 (JWT Best Current Practices) is short and worth reading in full. The validation checklist it implies:

1. **Pin the algorithm.** Accept only the algorithms you expect, configured on the verifier, never taken from the token header.
2. **Pick the key by `kid` from a trusted source** (your configured JWKS URL), never from a URL inside the token (`jku`, `x5u`) unless it matches an allowlist.
3. Verify the signature.
4. Check `exp` and `nbf` with a small clock-skew allowance (30-60 seconds).
5. Check `iss` exactly matches the expected issuer.
6. Check `aud` contains *this* service. Without this, a token minted for a low-security service can be replayed against a high-security one.
7. Check `typ` where you can, and the scopes or roles the endpoint needs.

The famous attacks all come from skipping step 1 or 2:

- **`alg: none`**: the attacker removes the signature and sets `alg` to `none`. Old libraries accepted it.
- **Algorithm confusion (RS256 to HS256)**: the verifier is configured with the RSA public key. The attacker sets `alg: HS256` and signs the token with HMAC using the *public key as the secret*. A library that lets the header choose the algorithm will verify it successfully. Pinning `algorithms: ["RS256"]` kills it.
- **`kid` injection**: the `kid` is used in a file path or SQL query to look up the key. Treat it as untrusted input.
- **Unverified decode**: calling `jwt.decode()` (which does not verify) instead of `jwt.verify()` and trusting the result. This one shows up in real code reviews constantly.

Here is verification done properly with the `jose` library in Node:

```ts
import { createRemoteJWKSet, jwtVerify, errors } from "jose";

const JWKS = createRemoteJWKSet(new URL("https://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json"));

export async function verifyAccessToken(token: string) {
  try {
    const { payload } = await jwtVerify(token, JWKS, {
      issuer: "https://auth.example.com",
      audience: "https://api.example.com",
      algorithms: ["RS256"],
      typ: "at+jwt",
      clockTolerance: "30s",
    });
    return { userId: payload.sub!, scope: String(payload.scope ?? "").split(" ") };
  } catch (e) {
    if (e instanceof errors.JWTExpired) throw new Unauthorized("token_expired");
    throw new Unauthorized("invalid_token");
  }
}

class Unauthorized extends Error {}
```

`createRemoteJWKSet` caches keys and refetches when it sees an unknown `kid`, which is exactly the behaviour you need during rotation.

## Short-lived access, long-lived refresh

Because access tokens cannot easily be revoked, keep them short: **5 to 15 minutes** is typical. To avoid logging the user in every 15 minutes, the client also holds a **refresh token**: long-lived (days to weeks), opaque, stored server-side by the authorization server, and only ever sent to the token endpoint.

**Refresh token rotation** (recommended for public clients by the OAuth 2.0 Security BCP, RFC 9700) means every refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. The clever part is **reuse detection**:

```text
family F: RT1 -> (refresh) -> RT2 -> (refresh) -> RT3
attacker stole RT2 earlier and uses it after the user already rotated to RT3:
   token endpoint sees RT2 is already used  ->  revoke the whole family F
   both the attacker and the user are logged out; the user logs in again
```

Implementation notes: store refresh tokens hashed, with `familyId`, `parentId`, `usedAt`, `expiresAt`, and an absolute family lifetime. Allow a tiny grace window (a few seconds) for the legitimate race where two browser tabs refresh at once, or serialise refreshes on the client. Auth0's documentation on refresh token rotation describes the same model.

## Revocation strategies

You have several options, from cheapest to strongest:

1. **Short expiry only.** Logout deletes the refresh token; access tokens die within minutes. Fine for many apps.
2. **Denylist by `jti`.** On logout or compromise, put the `jti` in a store (Redis with TTL equal to remaining lifetime). Verifiers check it. You have reintroduced a lookup, but only against a small set.
3. **Token version per user.** Store `tokenVersion` on the user, embed it as a claim, bump it on password change or "log out everywhere". Verifiers compare (cacheable for seconds).
4. **Introspection (RFC 7662).** Use opaque access tokens and ask the authorization server on each request (with caching). You lose statelessness but gain instant revocation.

Be honest in interviews: if you need instant revocation of every token, you need state somewhere. JWTs move the lookup, they do not delete it.

## Where to store tokens in a browser

- **`localStorage`**: readable by any script on the page, so any XSS steals the token for use elsewhere. Avoid for long-lived tokens.
- **In memory**: lost on reload; combine with a refresh token in an `HttpOnly` cookie scoped to the refresh endpoint.
- **Backend for frontend (BFF)**: the browser has only a session cookie; the BFF holds tokens server-side. This is the direction the IETF "OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications" guidance points towards for sensitive apps.

## Trade-offs and when not to use JWTs

Use JWTs for: service-to-service auth, APIs consumed by many services that should not all call an auth server, federated identity (OIDC ID tokens), and short-lived signed capabilities (signed download links). Do not use them as a drop-in replacement for a first-party web session: you get a larger cookie, harder revocation and more ways to get it wrong, for a lookup you could have done in under a millisecond. A token of 1-2 KB on every request also adds up on mobile.

## Common mistakes and debugging

- Verifying with `decode` instead of `verify`, or not passing `algorithms`.
- Not checking `aud`, so tokens for one API work on another.
- Hour-long or day-long access tokens with no revocation path.
- Personal data or internal flags in the payload, assuming it is hidden.
- One HS256 secret shared by ten services: any of them can mint admin tokens.
- No `kid`, so rotation means a flag day where all tokens break.
- Debugging: decode the token locally (never paste production tokens into a website), compare `iss`/`aud` byte for byte (trailing slashes matter), check server clocks with NTP, and log the verification error type, not the token.

## In the interview

**What they probe:** do you know the token is readable, what exactly must be validated, why algorithm pinning matters, how refresh rotation and reuse detection work, and whether you can reason about revocation honestly.

**A 60-second answer outline:**
1. Header, payload, signature; base64url, signed not encrypted.
2. Verify with a pinned algorithm and a key from a trusted JWKS by `kid`; check `exp`, `nbf`, `iss`, `aud`, `typ`, scopes.
3. Short-lived access tokens (5-15 min), rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection.
4. Revocation needs state: denylist by `jti`, a per-user token version, or introspection.
5. For a first-party browser app I would still prefer a session cookie or a BFF.

**Follow-ups to expect:** "Explain the RS256/HS256 confusion attack"; "How do you rotate signing keys with zero downtime?"; "Where would you store tokens in a SPA?"; "How do you log a user out everywhere?"
keyPoints: A JWT payload is base64url-encoded, not encrypted; anyone holding the token can read it.
Pin accepted algorithms on the verifier and pick keys by kid from a trusted JWKS; never let the token choose.
Always check exp, nbf, iss, aud and typ; a missing aud check lets tokens for one API work on another.
Keep access tokens short (5-15 min) and rotate refresh tokens with reuse detection that revokes the whole family.
Instant revocation needs state: a jti denylist, a per-user token version, or introspection.
interview: What is inside a JWT, and what exactly must a server check when it validates one?
Explain the JWT algorithm confusion attack and how to prevent it.
How do refresh token rotation and reuse detection work, and how would you revoke JWTs?

check.q: A verifier is configured with an RSA public key but reads the algorithm from the token header. What can an attacker do?
options: Nothing, because RSA public keys cannot sign
Sign a forged token with HS256 using the public key as the HMAC secret
check.why: This is algorithm confusion: with alg switched to HS256, the library uses the public key bytes as an HMAC secret, which the attacker knows. Pinning algorithms to RS256 prevents it.

check.q: Why do refresh token rotation schemes revoke the whole token family when an old refresh token is reused?
options: Reuse means two parties hold tokens from the same chain, so one of them is probably an attacker
Because access tokens cannot be verified after rotation
The OAuth spec forbids more than one refresh per hour
check.why: A legitimate client only uses each refresh token once. Seeing a used one again signals theft, and since you cannot tell which party is legitimate, you revoke the family and force re-login.

check.q: Which claim check stops a token minted for the low-risk notifications API from being accepted by the payments API?
check.why: aud names the intended recipient. Each API must verify that its own identifier is in aud, otherwise any valid token from the same issuer is accepted.

lessons.title: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect: code flow, PKCE, client credentials and ID tokens
lessons.summary: Delegation versus identity, the authorization code flow with PKCE step by step, client credentials, validating OIDC ID tokens, scopes, and the misconfigurations attackers exploit.
lessons.body:
## The core idea

**OAuth 2.0 is a delegation protocol**: it lets a user grant an application limited access to their resources on another service ("let this calendar app read my Google Calendar") without handing over their password. The app receives an **access token** scoped to what the user approved. OAuth by itself does not tell the app *who* the user is.

**OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0.** It adds the `openid` scope, an **ID token** (a signed JWT describing the authentication event and the user), a `userinfo` endpoint and discovery metadata. "Sign in with Google" is OIDC; "let this app access your Drive" is OAuth.

The four roles, in OAuth vocabulary:

- **Resource owner**: the user.
- **Client**: the application asking for access (your web app, mobile app or backend job).
- **Authorization server (AS)**: issues tokens after authenticating the user and getting consent (Auth0, Okta, Entra ID, Keycloak, Google).
- **Resource server (RS)**: the API that accepts access tokens.

Clients are **confidential** (can keep a secret, such as a server-side web app) or **public** (cannot: SPAs, mobile and desktop apps).

## Authorization code flow with PKCE

This is the flow to use for essentially every user-facing client in 2026. The OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice (RFC 9700, published January 2025) requires PKCE for public clients and recommends it for confidential ones, and the OAuth 2.1 draft makes it mandatory. The implicit flow and the resource owner password grant are deprecated.

```text
Client                         Browser                       Authorization server        API
  | create code_verifier (random 43-128 chars)                    |                       |
  | code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier)); state; nonce    |                       |
  |--- 302 /authorize?response_type=code&client_id&redirect_uri   |                       |
  |        &scope=openid profile orders:read&state&nonce          |                       |
  |        &code_challenge&code_challenge_method=S256 ----------->|                       |
  |                               user logs in, consents          |                       |
  |<-- 302 redirect_uri?code=abc&state=... -----------------------|                       |
  | check state matches                                           |                       |
  |--- POST /token  grant_type=authorization_code&code=abc        |                       |
  |       &redirect_uri&code_verifier (+ client auth if confidential) ------------------->|
  |<-- { access_token, id_token, refresh_token, expires_in } -----|                       |
  | validate id_token (sig, iss, aud, exp, nonce)                 |                       |
  |--- GET /orders  Authorization: Bearer <access_token> ---------------------------------->|
```

Why each piece exists:

- **The code is a short-lived, one-time intermediate.** Tokens never travel in the URL, where they would end up in browser history, logs and `Referer` headers.
- **PKCE** binds the code to the client instance that started the flow. An attacker who intercepts the code (a malicious app registered for the same custom URL scheme on mobile, or a leaked log line) cannot redeem it without the `code_verifier`, which never left the client. Always use `S256`, not `plain`.
- **`state`** is a CSRF defence for the redirect: it ties the callback to a login the user actually started. With PKCE in place it is still useful to carry app state and detect mismatched responses.
- **`nonce`** (OIDC) is echoed inside the ID token so the client can detect replayed ID tokens.
- **Exact `redirect_uri` matching** at the AS stops attackers from redirecting codes to their own domain.

A minimal PKCE pair in Node:

```ts
import { randomBytes, createHash } from "node:crypto";

const b64url = (b: Buffer) => b.toString("base64url");

export function createPkce() {
  const verifier = b64url(randomBytes(32));                        // 43 chars
  const challenge = b64url(createHash("sha256").update(verifier).digest());
  return { verifier, challenge, method: "S256" as const };
}
```

In practice use a certified library (`openid-client` for Node, Auth.js-style frameworks, or your provider's SDK) rather than hand-rolling the flow; but you should be able to explain every parameter it sends.

## Client credentials flow

For machine-to-machine calls there is no user. The client authenticates directly to the token endpoint and receives an access token representing itself:

```bash
curl -s https://auth.example.com/oauth/token \
  -u "$CLIENT_ID:$CLIENT_SECRET" \
  -d grant_type=client_credentials \
  -d scope="invoices:write" \
  -d audience=https://billing.example.com
```

Notes: cache the token until shortly before `expires_in` (do not fetch a new one per request), scope it narrowly, and prefer stronger client authentication than a shared secret where available: `private_key_jwt` (the client signs a JWT assertion) or mutual TLS (RFC 8705), which also lets the AS issue certificate-bound tokens that are useless if stolen.

Other grants you should recognise: **device authorization** (RFC 8628, the "enter this code on your phone" flow for TVs and CLIs), **refresh token**, and **token exchange** (RFC 8693, a service swapping a user's token for a downscoped token to call another service).

## OIDC ID tokens

An ID token is a JWT *for the client*, describing who logged in and how:

```json
{
  "iss": "https://accounts.example.com",
  "sub": "248289761001",
  "aud": "my-client-id",
  "exp": 1790003600,
  "iat": 1790000000,
  "nonce": "n-0S6_WzA2Mj",
  "auth_time": 1789999990,
  "amr": ["pwd", "otp"],
  "email": "ana@example.com",
  "email_verified": true
}
```

The client must validate the signature (keys from the provider's JWKS, found via `/.well-known/openid-configuration`), `iss`, `aud` equals its own client id, `exp`, and `nonce`. Then it identifies the user by the pair **(`iss`, `sub`)**, which is stable and unique. **Email is not an identifier**: users change emails, some providers let users set unverified emails, and linking accounts by email has caused real account-takeover bugs. Only trust email for linking when `email_verified` is true and the provider is authoritative for that domain.

ID tokens are not access tokens. Do not send them to your API as bearer credentials: their audience is the client, not the API.

## Scopes and claims

Scopes are coarse permission strings the client requests and the user consents to: `openid`, `profile`, `email`, `offline_access` (ask for a refresh token), and API-specific ones like `orders:read`. Two rules of thumb:

- Scopes describe what the *client* may do on the user's behalf. They are not a replacement for your own authorization: a token with `orders:read` still only lets user 42 read user 42's orders.
- Request the minimum and use incremental consent for more sensitive scopes later.

## Common misconfigurations (the ones that end up in bug bounty reports)

1. **Loose redirect URI matching** (prefix or wildcard), combined with an open redirect on the client domain, leaks codes or tokens to the attacker.
2. **Missing `state` or `nonce` checks**, enabling login CSRF (the victim is logged into the attacker's account) or ID token replay.
3. **Using the implicit flow** or putting tokens in URL fragments.
4. **Not validating `aud`** on access tokens at the API, so a token issued for any client of the same AS works.
5. **Account linking by unverified email** across providers.
6. **Tokens in `localStorage`** for a high-value app; a single XSS exfiltrates them.
7. **Long-lived bearer tokens** with no rotation and broad scopes.
8. **Mix-up attacks** when a client talks to several authorization servers and cannot tell which one sent a response; the `iss` parameter in the authorization response (RFC 9207) addresses this.
9. **Trusting the `alg` from discovery or token headers** rather than pinning.

## Architecture choices for web apps

For a SPA, the safest common pattern is a **backend for frontend**: the BFF is a confidential client that runs the code flow, keeps tokens server-side, and gives the browser an `HttpOnly` session cookie. The browser never sees an access token. The alternative, a pure SPA public client with PKCE, works but must keep tokens in memory and use refresh token rotation.

For mobile apps, use the system browser (ASWebAuthenticationSession on iOS, Custom Tabs on Android), never an embedded WebView, as RFC 8252 describes; and use claimed HTTPS redirect URIs (universal or app links) where possible.

## Trade-offs and when not to use it

Running your own authorization server is a serious commitment (key management, consent, discovery, compliance). For most products, use a managed provider or Keycloak and focus on integrating correctly. You also do not need OAuth for a first-party app with its own username and password: a session is simpler. OAuth earns its keep when you have third-party clients, many services or federated login.

## Debugging

Read the provider's discovery document first. Decode tokens locally and compare `iss`, `aud` and `azp` with what your verifier expects. Most "invalid_grant" errors are a reused or expired code, a `redirect_uri` mismatch between the authorize and token calls, or a missing or wrong `code_verifier`.

## In the interview

**What they probe:** the difference between OAuth and OIDC, the code flow with PKCE parameter by parameter, why implicit is dead, ID token versus access token, and real-world misconfigurations.

**A 60-second answer outline:**
1. OAuth is delegated authorization; OIDC adds authentication with an ID token.
2. Code flow plus PKCE: verifier and S256 challenge, `state`, `nonce`, exact redirect URIs, code exchanged at the token endpoint.
3. Validate the ID token (sig, iss, aud, exp, nonce) and identify users by `iss` + `sub`.
4. Client credentials for service-to-service, with cached, narrowly scoped tokens.
5. For SPAs prefer a BFF so tokens stay server-side.

**Follow-ups to expect:** "What attack does PKCE stop?"; "Why not use the ID token to call your API?"; "How would you secure the CLI login for your product?" (device flow or loopback redirect with PKCE); "What breaks if redirect URIs allow wildcards?"
keyPoints: OAuth 2.0 delegates access with scoped access tokens; OpenID Connect adds identity via a signed ID token.
Use authorization code + PKCE (S256) for every user-facing client; implicit and password grants are deprecated.
Identify users by (iss, sub), never by email alone, and never send ID tokens to your API.
Client credentials is for machine-to-machine: cache tokens, scope narrowly, prefer private_key_jwt or mTLS.
Most real breaches are misconfigurations: loose redirect URIs, missing state/nonce, no aud check, email-based linking.

The token endpoint requires the original code_verifier, which never left the legitimate app

lessons.title: Passwords and MFA: Argon2id, credential stuffing, TOTP and passkeys
lessons.summary: Storing passwords with Argon2id or bcrypt, NIST-style policy, defending against credential stuffing, how TOTP works and why WebAuthn passkeys are phishing-resistant.
lessons.body:
## The core idea

Passwords fail in two ways: **your database leaks** and attackers crack the stored hashes offline, or **users reuse passwords** that leaked elsewhere and attackers replay them against your login (credential stuffing). Good password handling addresses the first with slow, salted, memory-hard hashing, and the second with breached-password checks, rate limiting and, above all, a second factor that the attacker does not have. The strongest current answer, passkeys built on WebAuthn, removes the shared secret altogether and is phishing-resistant by design.

## Storing passwords: slow hashes, not fast ones

SHA-256 is designed to be fast; a modern GPU computes billions of SHA-256 hashes per second, so an 8-character password hashed with SHA-256 (even salted) falls quickly. Password hashing functions are deliberately slow and, ideally, **memory-hard**, so parallel hardware gains much less.

The OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet gives current minimums:

| Algorithm | Recommended minimum (OWASP) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Argon2id** | m = 19 MiB, t = 2 iterations, p = 1 | First choice. Memory-hard, winner of the Password Hashing Competition, specified in RFC 9106 |
| scrypt | N = 2^17, r = 8, p = 1 | Memory-hard; fine if Argon2id is unavailable |
| bcrypt | work factor 10 or more | Truncates input at 72 bytes; widely available |
| PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 | 600,000 iterations | Use when FIPS compliance is required |

What a stored hash looks like (a PHC string carries algorithm, parameters and salt, so you can upgrade parameters later):

```text
$argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$c29tZXNhbHRzb21lc2FsdA$J6...base64 hash...
```

```ts
import argon2 from "argon2";

const PARAMS = { type: argon2.argon2id, memoryCost: 19456, timeCost: 2, parallelism: 1 };

export async function hashPassword(pw: string) {
  return argon2.hash(pw, PARAMS);                  // random salt generated for you
}

export async function verifyPassword(stored: string, pw: string) {
  const ok = await argon2.verify(stored, pw);
  const needsRehash = ok && argon2.needsRehash(stored, PARAMS);
  return { ok, needsRehash };                      // rehash on successful login when params change
}
```

Key details:

- **Salt** (unique random per password, stored alongside) defeats precomputed rainbow tables and makes identical passwords hash differently. Libraries handle this.
- **Pepper** (an extra secret held outside the database, for example in a KMS or as an HMAC key applied before hashing) means a database-only leak is not crackable. It adds key-management burden; useful for high-value systems.
- **Tune for your hardware.** Aim for a hash time that is acceptable for login latency and CPU (tens to a few hundred milliseconds), and remember that a login endpoint doing expensive hashing is a denial-of-service target, so rate limit it.
- **Upgrade transparently.** On successful login, if `needsRehash`, store a new hash. For legacy MD5 or SHA-1 hashes, you can wrap them (`argon2id(sha1(pw))`) immediately rather than waiting for every user to log in.
- Do not encrypt passwords. You never need to decrypt them.

## Password policy: what NIST actually says

NIST SP 800-63B (revision 4, finalised in 2025) moved away from the old rules most people remember:

- Length matters more than composition: at least 15 characters when the password is the only factor, at least 8 when it is part of MFA. Allow at least 64 characters and all printable characters, including spaces.
- **No composition rules** (one uppercase, one symbol) and **no periodic forced rotation**; force a change only on evidence of compromise.
- **Check new passwords against known-breached lists** and common or context-specific words.
- Allow paste and password managers.

Checking against breaches without sending the password anywhere: Have I Been Pwned's Pwned Passwords API uses **k-anonymity**. You SHA-1 the password, send only the first 5 hex characters, receive all suffixes in that range, and compare locally.

```ts
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";

export async function isBreached(pw: string) {
  const sha1 = createHash("sha1").update(pw).digest("hex").toUpperCase();
  const prefix = sha1.slice(0, 5), suffix = sha1.slice(5);
  const res = await fetch(`https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/${prefix}`, { headers: { "Add-Padding": "true" } });
  const body = await res.text();
  return body.split(/\r?\n/).some((line) => line.startsWith(suffix) && !line.endsWith(":0"));
}
```

## Credential stuffing and online attacks

Credential stuffing uses millions of leaked email/password pairs, distributed across residential proxies, at a low rate per IP. Per-IP limits alone do not stop it. A layered defence:

1. **MFA**, which defeats replayed passwords outright.
2. **Breached-password checks** at signup, password change, and optionally at login.
3. **Rate limits on several keys**: per account (slow down after N failures, with exponential backoff rather than hard lockout, which itself becomes a denial-of-service tool), per IP and per IP range or ASN, and global failure-rate alarms.
4. **Bot signals**: device or browser fingerprints, CAPTCHA or proof-of-work challenges only when risk is high.
5. **Uniform responses**: the same error message and similar timing for "no such user" and "wrong password" to avoid account enumeration (hash a dummy password when the user does not exist).
6. **Notify users** of new-device logins and offer "this wasn't me".

## Second factors

### TOTP

Time-based one-time passwords (RFC 6238) build on HOTP (RFC 4226): the server and the authenticator app share a secret; the code is HMAC(secret, floor(unixTime / 30)), truncated to 6 digits.

```text
enrol:   server generates 160-bit secret -> otpauth://totp/App:ana?secret=BASE32&issuer=App -> QR code
         user scans, types current code -> server verifies -> store secret encrypted
login:   code == TOTP(secret, T) for T in {now-1, now, now+1} steps   (small skew window)
         remember the last used step to block replay within the window
```

Store TOTP secrets encrypted (they are shared secrets, unlike password hashes), rate-limit attempts (a 6-digit code has only a million possibilities), and issue one-time **recovery codes** at enrolment, stored hashed.

TOTP's weakness: it is **phishable**. A real-time phishing proxy (tools like Evilginx do this) relays the password and the code to the real site within the 30-second window and steals the resulting session. SMS codes are weaker still (SIM swaps, SS7 interception) and NIST classes SMS as a restricted authenticator.

### WebAuthn and passkeys

WebAuthn (a W3C standard, with FIDO2's CTAP for external authenticators) replaces shared secrets with public-key cryptography:

```text
register: server sends challenge + rpId ("example.com") + user id
          authenticator creates a key pair scoped to rpId, keeps the private key
          returns public key + credential id (+ attestation) -> server stores them
login:    server sends random challenge
          browser checks the page origin matches rpId, authenticator signs
          (challenge + origin + rpId hash + counter) after user verification (biometric/PIN)
          server verifies signature with stored public key, checks challenge, origin, rpId
```

Why it is phishing-resistant: the **browser** puts the real origin into the signed data and only offers credentials for the matching relying party. A look-alike domain cannot obtain a valid assertion for `example.com`, no matter how convincing the page. The server stores only public keys, so a database leak gives attackers nothing to replay.

**Passkeys** are discoverable WebAuthn credentials, usually synced across a user's devices by the platform (iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, password managers), so losing a phone does not lose the account. They can act as a single step that is both possession and user verification. Use a maintained library (SimpleWebAuthn for Node, `py_webauthn` for Python) rather than parsing CBOR yourself. passkeys.dev and the webauthn.guide site are good starting points.

## Trade-offs

- Argon2id parameters trade login latency and server CPU/memory against attacker cost; very high memory settings can exhaust a small container under a login burst.
- Mandatory MFA increases support load (lost devices); recovery flows become the weakest link, so protect them as strongly as login (recovery codes, re-verification, cooling-off periods for changes).
- Passkeys give the best security and UX but need fallback paths during migration, and account recovery still has to be designed.

## Common mistakes

- Fast hashes (MD5, SHA-1, plain SHA-256) or a single global salt.
- bcrypt with inputs over 72 bytes silently truncated (pre-hash with care, or use Argon2id).
- Hard lockout after 5 attempts, letting anyone lock out any user.
- Different error messages or response times that reveal which emails exist.
- TOTP secrets stored in plaintext, no replay protection, unlimited guesses.
- Password reset tokens that are long-lived, reusable or stored unhashed, or a reset that does not invalidate existing sessions.

## In the interview

**What they probe:** whether you know why fast hashes fail, the current algorithm and parameters, how credential stuffing differs from brute force, and why WebAuthn beats TOTP.

**A 60-second answer outline:**
1. Hash with Argon2id (OWASP minimum m=19 MiB, t=2, p=1), unique salt, PHC format, rehash on login when parameters change.
2. NIST-style policy: length, no composition rules or forced rotation, breached-password checks.
3. Credential stuffing: MFA, breach checks, multi-key rate limiting with backoff, bot signals, uniform errors.
4. MFA: TOTP is good but phishable; WebAuthn/passkeys are origin-bound and phishing-resistant.

**Follow-ups to expect:** "Why is bcrypt's 72-byte limit a problem?"; "How do you migrate a million MD5 hashes?"; "How does a phishing proxy defeat TOTP but not passkeys?"; "Design account recovery for a passkey-only account."
keyPoints: Use Argon2id (OWASP minimum m=19 MiB, t=2, p=1) with a unique salt; never fast hashes like SHA-256 or MD5.
Follow NIST SP 800-63B: favour length, drop composition rules and forced rotation, block breached passwords.
Credential stuffing is distributed and low-rate; MFA, breach checks and multi-key rate limits beat per-IP limits.
TOTP is HMAC over a 30-second time step: a real improvement, but phishable through real-time proxies.
WebAuthn passkeys sign an origin-bound challenge, so look-alike phishing sites cannot get a usable assertion.

check.q: Why is a salted SHA-256 hash a poor way to store passwords?
options: It is fast, so attackers can test billions of guesses per second on GPUs
Salts cannot be stored next to hashes
check.why: Salts stop rainbow tables, but SHA-256's speed lets offline attackers brute-force weak passwords cheaply. Slow, memory-hard functions like Argon2id raise the cost per guess.

check.q: How does the Pwned Passwords range API let you check a password without revealing it?
options: You send the full bcrypt hash
You send the first 5 hex characters of the SHA-1 hash and compare returned suffixes locally
The password is sent over TLS and deleted immediately
You send the password encrypted with the API's public key
check.why: This is k-anonymity: the prefix matches hundreds of hashes, and the comparison against the full hash happens on your server.

check.q: A real-time phishing proxy relays a user's password and 6-digit TOTP code to the real site. Which factor would have stopped it?
check.why: WebAuthn assertions include the origin checked by the browser, so a credential for example.com cannot be used from the phishing domain.

lessons.title: Authorization: RBAC, ABAC, ReBAC (Zanzibar), tenant isolation and IDOR
lessons.summary: Choosing an authorization model, how Zanzibar-style relationship checks work, enforcing multi-tenant isolation with scoped queries and row-level security, and killing IDOR bugs.
lessons.body:
## The core idea

**Authentication answers "who are you?"; authorization answers "may you do this, to this thing, right now?"** Authentication happens once per session. Authorization happens on every request, for every object, and it is where most real-world breaches live: Broken Access Control is number one in the OWASP Top 10, and Broken Object Level Authorization is number one in the OWASP API Security Top 10.

Every authorization decision has the same shape:

```text
decision = allow?( subject, action, resource, context )
           subject:  user 42, roles [editor], tenant acme, mfa=true
           action:   "invoice.approve"
           resource: invoice 981, tenant acme, owner 17, amount 12000
           context:  time, IP, device, request risk
```

Models differ in what information they use to decide. Architectures differ in *where* the decision is made and *where* it is enforced. Get both right and, crucially, make the check impossible to forget.

## RBAC: role-based access control

Users get roles; roles carry permissions.

```text
user ana  -> role "billing-admin" -> permissions { invoice.read, invoice.approve, refund.create }
user ben  -> role "viewer"        -> permissions { invoice.read }
```

```ts
const ROLE_PERMS: Record<Role, ReadonlySet<Permission>> = {
  viewer: new Set(["invoice.read"]),
  "billing-admin": new Set(["invoice.read", "invoice.approve", "refund.create"]),
};

export function can(user: { roles: Role[] }, perm: Permission) {
  return user.roles.some((r) => ROLE_PERMS[r].has(perm));
}
```

**Strengths:** easy to understand and audit ("who can approve invoices?"), maps to org charts, cheap to evaluate. **Weaknesses:** it answers "can editors edit documents?" but not "can Ana edit *this* document?". Teams patch that with ever more specific roles (`editor-project-17`), which is **role explosion**. Check for permissions in code, never role names (`can(user, "invoice.approve")`, not `user.role === "admin"`), so roles can change without code changes.

## ABAC: attribute-based access control

Decisions are policies over attributes of the subject, resource, action and environment:

```text
allow invoice.approve if
    subject.department == "finance"
    and resource.tenant == subject.tenant
    and resource.amount <= subject.approvalLimit
    and context.mfaAge < 15 minutes
```

**Strengths:** expressive, handles fine-grained and contextual rules (limits, time, location, data classification) without new roles. **Weaknesses:** harder to answer "who can access X?" (you would have to evaluate policies over all users), harder to audit, and policies can become unreadable code. Policy engines help: **Open Policy Agent** with the Rego language, and **AWS Cedar**, a policy language designed to be analysable (Amazon Verified Permissions uses it).

## ReBAC and Google Zanzibar

Relationship-based access control decides based on a graph of relationships: "Ana can view doc 7 because she is a member of team Design, which is an editor of folder Q3, which is the parent of doc 7." This is how Google Drive, GitHub and Notion-style sharing work.

Google's **Zanzibar** paper (USENIX ATC 2019) describes the system behind Drive, YouTube, Calendar and others. Its core ideas:

- Permissions are stored as **relation tuples**: `object#relation@subject`, for example `doc:7#viewer@user:ana` or `doc:7#parent@folder:q3` or `folder:q3#editor@team:design#member`.
- A **namespace configuration** defines how relations compose, such as "viewers include editors" and "viewers of a doc include viewers of its parent folder".
- The API answers `check(object, relation, user)`, plus `expand` and reverse lookups ("which docs can Ana see?").
- **Zookies** are consistency tokens: when content changes, the client stores a zookie with it, and later checks are evaluated at a snapshot at least as fresh, avoiding the "new enemy" problem (removing someone's access, then adding content they should not see, and a stale check still letting them in).

Open-source implementations inspired by Zanzibar include **OpenFGA** (CNCF project, originally from Auth0) and **SpiceDB** (AuthZed). An OpenFGA-style model:

```text
model
  schema 1.1
type user
type team
  relations
    define member: [user]
type folder
  relations
    define editor: [user, team#member]
    define viewer: [user, team#member] or editor
type doc
  relations
    define parent: [folder]
    define editor: [user] or editor from parent
    define viewer: [user] or editor or viewer from parent
```

**Strengths:** natural for sharing, hierarchies and groups; one central service for many products; reverse queries for listing. **Weaknesses:** a new distributed system to run, data duplication between your DB and the tuple store (you must keep them in sync, often via an outbox), and listing/filtering large result sets is hard.

Most real systems are hybrids: RBAC for coarse admin features, ReBAC for sharing, ABAC conditions for limits and context.

## Multi-tenant isolation

In a SaaS product the most damaging authorization bug is a **cross-tenant leak**: customer A sees customer B's data. Defence in depth:

1. **Tenant from the session, never from the request.** The tenant id comes from the authenticated principal; a `tenantId` in the body or URL is at most a hint that must match.
2. **Every query is tenant-scoped** by construction: a repository layer that requires `tenantId`, or an ORM middleware that injects it.
3. **Database-enforced isolation as a backstop.** Postgres **row-level security** can enforce it even if application code forgets:

```sql
ALTER TABLE invoices ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE invoices FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON invoices
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid)
  WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid);

-- per request, inside the transaction:
SET LOCAL app.tenant_id = 'a1b2...';
```

Note that table owners and superusers bypass RLS unless `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` is set and the app connects as a non-owner role. With connection pooling, use `SET LOCAL` inside a transaction so the setting cannot leak to the next request on the same connection.

4. **Stronger isolation tiers** for high-value customers: schema per tenant or database per tenant, at the cost of operational complexity and migrations across many databases.
5. **Tenant-aware caches and search indexes.** Cache keys and vector or search queries must include the tenant; this is a frequent leak.

## IDOR and BOLA

An **insecure direct object reference** happens when an endpoint takes an object id from the client and returns or modifies the object without checking that the caller may access it:

```ts
// vulnerable: any logged-in user can read any invoice by changing the id
app.get("/api/invoices/:id", requireAuth, async (req, res) => {
  res.json(await db.invoice.findUnique({ where: { id: req.params.id } }));
});

// fixed: scope the lookup to the caller, and return 404 rather than 403 to avoid confirming existence
app.get("/api/invoices/:id", requireAuth, async (req, res) => {
  const inv = await db.invoice.findFirst({
    where: { id: req.params.id, tenantId: req.user.tenantId },
  });
  if (!inv || !(await authz.check(req.user, "invoice.read", inv))) return res.sendStatus(404);
  res.json(inv);
});
```

Random UUIDs make ids harder to guess but are **not** an authorization control: ids leak through URLs, logs, emails and shared links. The fix is always an object-level check. Watch the variants: nested resources (`/projects/1/tasks/99` where task 99 belongs to project 2), bulk endpoints that accept arrays of ids, GraphQL resolvers that skip checks on nested fields, file download URLs, and write paths (mass assignment of `ownerId` or `tenantId`).

## Where to enforce

- **Policy decision point (PDP)**: the code or service that evaluates "allow?". **Policy enforcement point (PEP)**: the place that calls it and blocks the request.
- Enforce in the **service layer next to the data**, not only in the UI or the API gateway. The gateway can check coarse things (authenticated, has scope), but only the service knows who owns invoice 981.
- **Deny by default**: a new endpoint with no policy should fail closed.
- For lists, push filters into the query ("invoices where tenant = X and (owner = me or shared with my team)") instead of fetching everything and filtering in memory, which is slow and leaks via counts and pagination.
- **Test authorization**: a matrix of roles times endpoints, plus automated tests that call every endpoint as a user from another tenant and expect 404.

## Common mistakes

- Checking authorization in the frontend only, or only hiding buttons.
- Trusting `tenantId`, `userId` or `role` from the request body.
- Role-name checks scattered through the code.
- Forgetting the background-job and admin-tool paths, which often run with superuser access.
- Caching an authorization decision too long after a permission is revoked.

## In the interview

**What they probe:** whether you can pick a model for a product (RBAC versus ABAC versus ReBAC), whether you instinctively scope every object access, how you guarantee tenant isolation, and (senior) how a Zanzibar-style service works and its consistency trade-offs.

**A 60-second answer outline:**
1. Authorization is per request, per object, deny by default, enforced in the service next to the data.
2. RBAC for coarse capabilities, ReBAC for sharing and hierarchies, ABAC conditions for limits and context.
3. Multi-tenant: tenant from the session, scoped repositories, RLS as a backstop, tenant-aware caches.
4. IDOR: every lookup by id is also scoped by owner or tenant; UUIDs are not a control.
5. Test with cross-tenant and cross-role suites.

**Follow-ups to expect:** "Design permissions for Google Docs-style sharing"; "How do you list only the documents a user can see, at scale?"; "What is the new-enemy problem?"; "How would you migrate from hard-coded roles to a policy engine?"
keyPoints: Authorization is decided per request and per object, deny by default, enforced in the service next to the data.
RBAC is simple and auditable but explodes for per-object rules; ABAC adds attributes and context; ReBAC models sharing graphs.
Zanzibar stores relation tuples (object#relation@subject) and uses zookies to avoid the new-enemy problem.
Take the tenant from the session, scope every query, and use Postgres row-level security as a backstop.
IDOR is fixed by object-level checks on every lookup; random UUIDs are not an authorization control.

What is an IDOR vulnerability and how do you prevent it systematically?
How do you guarantee tenant isolation in a multi-tenant SaaS backend?

check.q: An endpoint GET /api/orders/:id loads the order by id after checking the user is logged in. The ids are random UUIDs. What is the status?
options: Safe, because UUIDs cannot be guessed
Vulnerable to IDOR, because there is no check that the order belongs to the caller
Safe if the endpoint uses HTTPS
check.why: Ids leak through URLs, logs and sharing. Without an object-level ownership or tenant check, any authenticated user who obtains an id can read the order.

check.q: Which model best fits Google Drive-style sharing with folders, groups and inherited permissions?
options: Pure RBAC with one role per folder
Access control lists stored in the frontend
ReBAC, for example a Zanzibar-style relation tuple store
check.why: Sharing is a graph of relationships (member of team, editor of folder, parent of doc). ReBAC evaluates those relations directly, which is what Zanzibar was built for.

check.q: With Postgres row-level security and a connection pool, why set the tenant with SET LOCAL inside a transaction?
options: SET LOCAL is faster than SET
The setting ends with the transaction, so it cannot leak to the next request reusing the pooled connection
check.why: A plain SET persists on the connection. With pooling, the next request on that connection could inherit another tenant's id; SET LOCAL scopes it to the transaction.

lessons.title: OWASP Top 10 (2025) with concrete exploits and fixes
lessons.summary: Every category of the OWASP Top 10:2025, from broken access control and SSRF to supply chain and exceptional conditions, each with a realistic exploit and the fix that removes the bug class.
lessons.body:
## The core idea

The **OWASP Top 10** is a ranked list of the most important categories of web application security risk, built from data contributed by testing organisations plus a community survey. It is not a checklist that makes you "secure", but it is the shared vocabulary interviewers, auditors and pen-testers use. The current edition is **OWASP Top 10:2025**, published in late 2025 and replacing the 2021 list.

| # | 2025 category | What changed since 2021 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A01 | Broken Access Control | Still number one; now also includes SSRF (previously its own A10) and CSRF |
| A02 | Security Misconfiguration | Up from A05 |
| A03 | Software Supply Chain Failures | New, broadens 2021's "Vulnerable and Outdated Components" |
| A04 | Cryptographic Failures | Down from A02 |
| A05 | Injection | Down from A03; still covers SQL, NoSQL, OS command injection and XSS |
| A06 | Insecure Design | Down from A04 |
| A07 | Authentication Failures | Renamed from "Identification and Authentication Failures" |
| A08 | Software or Data Integrity Failures | Same position |
| A09 | Security Logging and Alerting Failures | Renamed to stress alerting, not just logging |
| A10 | Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions | New: error handling, failing open, logic errors under abnormal conditions |

If an interviewer quotes the 2021 list, that is fine: the categories largely map. What they want is concrete examples and fixes, which is what the rest of this lesson gives you.

## A01 Broken Access Control (including SSRF)

The application lets a user act outside their intended permissions.

- **IDOR**: `GET /api/invoices/981` returns another customer's invoice because the handler never checks ownership.
- **Missing function-level checks**: `POST /api/admin/users/42/role` works for any logged-in user because only the admin UI hides the button.
- **Privilege escalation through mass assignment**: `PATCH /api/me {"role":"admin"}` is bound straight into the model.
- **CSRF**: a cross-site form triggers a state change using the victim's cookies.

Fix: deny by default, object-level checks in the service layer, explicit allowlists of writable fields, cross-tenant tests. (The authorization lesson goes deep on this.)

**SSRF** (server-side request forgery) sits here in 2025. Any feature where your server fetches a user-supplied URL (webhooks, link previews, "import from URL", PDF renderers, image proxies) can be pointed at internal targets:

```text
POST /api/preview { "url": "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/" }
server fetches cloud metadata -> returns temporary cloud credentials to the attacker
```

The 2019 Capital One breach involved SSRF against the EC2 metadata service. Defences:

1. Allowlist schemes (`https` only) and, where possible, destination hosts.
2. Resolve the hostname yourself and **reject private, loopback, link-local and metadata ranges** (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 127/8, 169.254/16, ::1, fc00::/7, and so on); then connect to the IP you validated, otherwise DNS rebinding swaps the address between check and use.
3. Re-validate on every redirect, or disable redirects.
4. Enforce timeouts and response size caps.
5. Network-level egress controls: run fetchers in a segment that cannot reach internal services; on AWS require IMDSv2, which needs a session token obtained via a PUT request.

## A02 Security Misconfiguration

Insecure defaults and forgotten settings: debug mode on in production (stack traces with secrets), default admin credentials, directory listing, an S3 bucket or Elasticsearch cluster open to the internet, permissive CORS (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin` reflecting any origin with credentials), missing security headers, verbose error pages, unused features enabled. XML parsers with external entities enabled (XXE) also land here.

Fix: hardened, repeatable configuration as code; separate prod and dev configs; automated scanning of cloud config (for example AWS Config rules, Prowler, Trivy for IaC); security headers by default; review of every exposed port and bucket.

## A03 Software Supply Chain Failures

Your code is mostly other people's code. Risks: known-vulnerable dependencies (Log4Shell, CVE-2021-44228, let attackers trigger remote code execution through a logged string), malicious packages via typosquatting or compromised maintainers (the 2024 `xz-utils` backdoor; repeated npm account takeovers), compromised build systems (SolarWinds), and unpinned CI actions.

Fix: lockfiles and pinned versions, automated dependency updates with review (Dependabot, Renovate), vulnerability scanning in CI, an SBOM, pinning GitHub Actions to commit SHAs, minimal CI token permissions, provenance and signing (Sigstore, SLSA levels), and a policy for how quickly critical CVEs are patched.

## A04 Cryptographic Failures

Sensitive data exposed through missing or weak cryptography: plaintext HTTP, passwords stored with MD5 or SHA-1, home-made encryption, ECB mode, hard-coded keys, predictable random numbers (`Math.random()` for reset tokens), disabled certificate validation (`rejectUnauthorized: false` in production), or reusing an AES-GCM nonce.

Fix: TLS everywhere with HSTS, Argon2id for passwords, vetted libraries and AEAD modes, keys in a KMS, CSPRNG for every token, data classification so you know what must be encrypted.

## A05 Injection

Untrusted data is interpreted as code or commands by an interpreter.

**SQL injection:**

```ts
// vulnerable
await db.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '${email}'`);
// email = "' OR '1'='1" returns every user

// fixed: parameterised query; the driver sends data separately from the SQL text
await db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1", [email]);
```

Identifiers (column names for sorting, table names) cannot be parameterised, so map them through an allowlist.

**NoSQL injection** in MongoDB: a JSON body of `{"email": {"$ne": null}, "password": {"$ne": null}}` turns an equality check into "any user". Validate types with a schema (zod) so `email` must be a string, and use sanitisation such as Mongoose's `sanitizeFilter`.

**OS command injection**: `exec("convert " + filename)` with `filename = "a.png; rm -rf /"`. Use `execFile` with an argument array and no shell, or better, a library.

**XSS** is injection into HTML or JavaScript. Use framework auto-escaping (React escapes text by default), never pass untrusted strings to `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` or `innerHTML`, sanitise with DOMPurify if you must render HTML, and add a strict Content Security Policy as defence in depth.

**Prompt injection** into LLM features is the newest member of the family: model output must be treated as untrusted, and tools the model can call must be authorised as if the user called them directly.

## A06 Insecure Design

Flaws that no amount of correct code fixes because the design itself is unsafe: a password reset that relies on security questions, a checkout that trusts the client-supplied price, a referral scheme with no limit on self-referrals, unlimited OTP attempts. Fix with threat modelling (STRIDE, abuse cases) during design, business-logic limits, and secure design patterns reused across teams.

## A07 Authentication Failures

Credential stuffing with no rate limiting or MFA, weak password storage, session ids in URLs, no session regeneration at login, missing logout invalidation, user enumeration via different error messages, and weak recovery flows. Fix: the sessions, JWT and passwords lessons in this track.

## A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures

Trusting code or data without verifying integrity: auto-update without signatures, CI pipelines that pull unverified artifacts, **insecure deserialisation** (Java `ObjectInputStream`, Python `pickle`, PHP `unserialize` on user input leading to remote code execution), and accepting client-side state (a signed cookie with a weak secret, a JWT without a pinned algorithm). Fix: sign and verify artifacts, never deserialise untrusted data into objects, use plain JSON with schema validation.

## A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures

Breaches go undetected for months because nobody logged or alerted. Log authentication events, authorization failures, admin actions, input validation failures at high rates and configuration changes; centralise logs; alert on patterns (spikes in 403s, logins from new countries for admins); protect logs from tampering; and never log secrets, tokens or passwords. An alert nobody reads is the same as no alert.

## A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions

New in 2025: what happens when things go wrong. Examples: an authorization check that throws on a timeout and the code **fails open** (`catch { return true }`), error messages leaking internals, unhandled promise rejections crashing the process (a denial of service), partial failures leaving a transaction half applied (money deducted, order not created), and resource exhaustion paths with no limits.

```ts
// fails open: an outage in the authz service grants access to everything
async function canAccess(user: User, doc: Doc) {
  try { return await authz.check(user, "view", doc); }
  catch { return true; }           // never do this
}
```

Fix: fail closed, use transactions or sagas for multi-step changes, return generic errors to clients while logging details internally, and test failure paths (chaos tests, fault injection).

## How to use the list in practice

- Map it onto your threat model and code review checklist; it is a starting point, not a standard. The **OWASP ASVS** (Application Security Verification Standard) is the testable requirements document if you need one.
- Automate what you can: SAST and dependency scanning in CI, DAST against staging, secret scanning on every push.
- Developers fix classes of bugs, not instances: a safe query builder, a single authorization helper, auto-escaping templates and an SSRF-safe HTTP client remove whole categories.

## In the interview

**What they probe:** can you name the categories, and more importantly give a concrete exploit and a concrete fix for each? Senior candidates are expected to talk about eliminating bug classes and about SSRF, supply chain and failure handling.

**A 60-second answer outline:**
1. Name the 2025 top three (access control, misconfiguration, supply chain) and mention injection and crypto.
2. Give one vivid example with its fix, such as IDOR fixed by scoped queries, or SSRF to cloud metadata fixed by IP validation and IMDSv2.
3. Explain how you prevent classes of bugs: secure defaults in shared libraries, CI scanning, threat modelling, logging with alerts.

**Follow-ups to expect:** "How would you build an SSRF-safe webhook sender?"; "Why are parameterised queries safe but escaping is fragile?"; "How do you respond to a new critical CVE in a transitive dependency?"; "Give an example of failing open."
keyPoints: OWASP Top 10:2025 puts Broken Access Control first, now including SSRF and CSRF; Software Supply Chain Failures is new at A03.
Injection is prevented by separating code from data: parameterised queries, schema-typed inputs, execFile without a shell, auto-escaping.
SSRF defences: scheme and host allowlists, resolve and block private ranges, pin the validated IP, re-check redirects, IMDSv2.
Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions (A10) is about failing closed and keeping multi-step changes atomic.
Fix bug classes with shared safe libraries, CI scanning and threat modelling rather than patching instances.
interview: Name the OWASP Top 10 categories you consider most important and give a concrete example and fix for each.
What is SSRF and how would you defend a feature that fetches user-supplied URLs?
How do you prevent SQL and NoSQL injection, and why is escaping not enough?

check.q: In the OWASP Top 10:2025, where does server-side request forgery (SSRF) belong?
options: It is still its own A10 category
It is part of A01 Broken Access Control
It is part of A04 Cryptographic Failures
check.why: The 2025 edition folds CWE-918 SSRF (and CSRF) into A01 Broken Access Control; A10 is now Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions.

check.q: A link-preview feature validates that a hostname resolves to a public IP, then calls fetch(url). How can an attacker still reach internal services?
options: By using HTTPS instead of HTTP
By sending a very long URL
Through DNS rebinding or a redirect, since the connection is not pinned to the validated IP and redirects are not re-checked
check.why: Validation and connection resolve the name separately, so the second lookup can return 127.0.0.1, and a 302 to an internal address bypasses a one-time check.

check.q: A login handler passes req.body straight into a MongoDB findOne. Which payload exploits it?
check.why: Operator objects turn equality checks into 'not null', matching the first user. Validating that fields are strings (for example with zod) blocks it.
