lessons.title: Secrets and applied crypto: KMS, envelope encryption, TLS, hash vs encrypt vs sign
lessons.summary: Picking the right primitive (hash, MAC, AEAD, signature), envelope encryption with a KMS, what TLS 1.3 guarantees, and running application secrets with scanning, rotation and workload identity.
lessons.body:
## The core idea

Backend security leans on a small set of cryptographic tools and on keeping a small set of secrets secret. Most failures are not broken algorithms; they are **the wrong tool for the job** (encrypting passwords, hashing for integrity without a key), **secrets in the wrong place** (in git, in env dumps, in logs) and **keys that never rotate**. This lesson covers the toolbox (hashing, MACs, encryption, signatures), how real systems manage keys (KMS and envelope encryption), what TLS actually guarantees, and how to handle application secrets.

## Hashing vs MAC vs encryption vs signing

| Tool | Key? | Reversible? | Guarantees | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cryptographic hash (SHA-256, SHA-3, BLAKE3) | No | No | Fixed-size fingerprint; collisions infeasible | Content addressing, dedupe, checksums against accidents, building block |
| Password hash (Argon2id, bcrypt) | No (salt, optional pepper) | No | Slow, salted, memory-hard | Storing passwords |
| MAC (HMAC-SHA256) | Shared secret | No | Integrity + authenticity between parties sharing the key | Webhook signatures, signed cookies, API request signing |
| Symmetric encryption (AES-256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) | Shared secret | Yes, with key | Confidentiality (+ integrity with AEAD) | Encrypting data at rest, field-level encryption |
| Asymmetric encryption / key exchange (RSA-OAEP, ECDH) | Public/private pair | Yes, with private key | Confidentiality to a key holder; establish shared keys | TLS key exchange, encrypting to a recipient |
| Digital signature (Ed25519, ECDSA, RSA-PSS) | Private signs, public verifies | No | Integrity + authenticity + non-repudiation; anyone can verify | JWTs, code signing, software updates |

The questions to ask: do I need to get the data back (encryption) or just compare it (hashing)? Who needs to verify, only me (MAC) or anyone (signature)? A plain hash of a message proves nothing about who sent it, because the attacker can recompute it; that is why webhooks use HMAC.

Verifying a webhook signature correctly:

```ts
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto";

export function verifyWebhook(rawBody: Buffer, header: string, secret: string, now = Date.now()) {
  // header format example: "t=1790000000,v1=hexsig"
  const parts = Object.fromEntries(header.split(",").map((p) => p.split("=") as [string, string]));
  const ts = Number(parts.t);
  if (!Number.isFinite(ts) || Math.abs(now / 1000 - ts) > 300) return false;   // replay window
  const expected = createHmac("sha256", secret).update(`${ts}.${rawBody}`).digest();
  const given = Buffer.from(parts.v1 ?? "", "hex");
  return given.length === expected.length && timingSafeEqual(given, expected);
}
```

Three details that matter: sign the **raw bytes** (re-serialised JSON will not match), include a **timestamp** to block replays (Stripe's webhook signatures follow this pattern), and compare in **constant time**.

## Symmetric encryption done right

Use an **AEAD** mode: AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305. They provide confidentiality and integrity together; tampered ciphertext fails to decrypt instead of producing garbage you might trust. Avoid ECB (identical blocks leak patterns) and unauthenticated CBC (padding oracle attacks).

The rule people break: **never reuse a nonce with the same key in GCM**. A repeated 96-bit nonce leaks the XOR of the two plaintexts and lets an attacker forge authentication tags. With random 96-bit nonces, NIST guidance limits you to about 2^32 encryptions per key; rotate keys well before that, or use XChaCha20-Poly1305 with 192-bit nonces for very high volumes.

```ts
import { randomBytes, createCipheriv, createDecipheriv } from "node:crypto";

export function encrypt(key: Buffer, plaintext: Buffer, aad: Buffer) {
  const iv = randomBytes(12);
  const c = createCipheriv("aes-256-gcm", key, iv);
  c.setAAD(aad);                                            // e.g. tenant id + record id
  const ct = Buffer.concat([c.update(plaintext), c.final()]);
  return Buffer.concat([iv, c.getAuthTag(), ct]);           // store iv | tag | ciphertext
}

export function decrypt(key: Buffer, blob: Buffer, aad: Buffer) {
  const iv = blob.subarray(0, 12), tag = blob.subarray(12, 28), ct = blob.subarray(28);
  const d = createDecipheriv("aes-256-gcm", key, iv);
  d.setAAD(aad);
  d.setAuthTag(tag);
  return Buffer.concat([d.update(ct), d.final()]);         // throws if tampered
}
```

**Associated data (AAD)** is authenticated but not encrypted. Binding the record id and tenant id means an attacker with database write access cannot swap one customer's encrypted field into another customer's row.

## KMS and envelope encryption

You do not want application servers holding long-lived master keys. A **key management service** (AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault's transit engine) keeps master keys inside HSM-backed infrastructure; you can ask it to encrypt, decrypt or generate keys, gated by IAM and recorded in audit logs, but the master key never leaves.

KMS calls are network round trips with request quotas and size limits (AWS KMS `Encrypt` accepts at most 4 KB of plaintext), so you do not send your data to KMS. Instead you use **envelope encryption**:

```text
encrypt:
  app -> KMS.GenerateDataKey(keyId=KEK)  ->  { plaintextDEK, encryptedDEK }
  ciphertext = AES-256-GCM(plaintextDEK, data)
  store { encryptedDEK, ciphertext, kekId } ; wipe plaintextDEK from memory

decrypt:
  app -> KMS.Decrypt(encryptedDEK) -> plaintextDEK   (IAM-checked, audit-logged)
  data = AES-256-GCM-decrypt(plaintextDEK, ciphertext)
```

- The **data encryption key (DEK)** encrypts data locally and fast; the **key encryption key (KEK)** in KMS only ever wraps DEKs.
- **Rotation is cheap**: rotating the KEK means re-wrapping small DEKs, not re-encrypting terabytes. AWS KMS automatic rotation keeps old key versions so existing ciphertexts still decrypt.
- **Blast radius is small**: a DEK per tenant, per file or per record means one leaked DEK exposes little.
- **Crypto-shredding**: deleting a tenant's DEK (or its KEK) renders their data unreadable everywhere, including backups, which helps with deletion requests.
- Cache decrypted DEKs briefly in memory to reduce KMS calls and cost; the AWS Encryption SDK implements this pattern.

## TLS: what it gives you

TLS provides **confidentiality, integrity and server authentication** for data in transit. TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446, 2018) simplified the protocol a lot; Cloudflare's write-up of RFC 8446 is a readable overview.

```text
ClientHello (supported ciphers, key share for X25519)  ->
                                <-  ServerHello (key share), {EncryptedExtensions,
                                     Certificate, CertificateVerify, Finished}
{Finished}, application data    ->
one round trip; everything after ServerHello is encrypted
```

- **Forward secrecy** is mandatory in 1.3: every connection uses an ephemeral (EC)DHE key exchange, so a later theft of the server's certificate key does not decrypt recorded traffic.
- Only AEAD cipher suites remain; RSA key transport, CBC suites, RC4 and compression are gone.
- **0-RTT resumption** saves a round trip but its early data can be **replayed**, so only allow it for idempotent requests.
- The server proves its identity with a certificate chain to a trusted CA; the client must validate the chain and hostname. Never disable verification in production code.
- **mTLS** adds a client certificate, giving strong service identity inside a cluster (service meshes such as Istio and Linkerd automate it, often with SPIFFE identities).
- **HSTS** (`Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains`) tells browsers to refuse plain HTTP, closing the first-request downgrade gap.
- Post-quantum key exchange is rolling out: hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM (Kyber) is already enabled by default in current Chrome, Firefox and at Cloudflare, protecting today's traffic against future decryption.

TLS protects the pipe, not the endpoints. Data is plaintext in your app, logs and database unless you encrypt it there too.

## Application secrets management

Secrets: database passwords, API keys, signing keys, OAuth client secrets, webhook secrets.

1. **Never commit secrets.** Use secret scanning (GitHub push protection, gitleaks, trufflehog) on every push. If a secret was ever committed, **rotate it**; rewriting history is not enough, because forks, clones and caches keep it.
2. **Store them in a secrets manager** (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Vault, Doppler, 1Password) rather than in config files. Inject at runtime with least-privilege IAM per service.
3. **Prefer no static secrets**: workload identity (IAM roles for service accounts, GCP Workload Identity, GitHub Actions OIDC federation to AWS/GCP) issues short-lived credentials automatically. Vault's dynamic database credentials create a user per lease and revoke it at expiry.
4. **Rotate** on a schedule and immediately on suspicion; design for two valid secrets during rotation (accept old and new, then remove old).
5. **Keep secrets out of logs, error messages, crash dumps, URLs and client bundles.** In Next.js, only variables prefixed `NEXT_PUBLIC_` reach the browser; anything with that prefix is public.
6. Environment variables are acceptable delivery but leak easily (process listings, debug endpoints, error reporters that dump `process.env`). Scrub them in error reporting.

## Common mistakes

- Using encryption where hashing is needed (passwords) or a plain hash where a MAC is needed (webhooks).
- AES-GCM with a fixed or counter nonce reused across restarts; hard-coded keys in source.
- `Math.random()` for tokens; use `crypto.randomBytes` or `crypto.randomUUID`.
- Comparing secrets with `===`.
- Treating base64 as encryption.
- `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0` copied from a Stack Overflow answer into production.
- No plan to rotate signing keys, so a leak means a long outage.

## In the interview

**What they probe:** whether you choose the right primitive, understand envelope encryption and why KMS exists, know what TLS 1.3 guarantees (and does not), and run secrets like an operator.

**A 60-second answer outline:**
1. Hash to fingerprint, password-hash to store passwords, MAC for shared-key integrity, sign for public verifiability, AEAD encrypt for confidentiality.
2. Envelope encryption: KMS-held KEK wraps per-tenant DEKs; data encrypted locally with AES-256-GCM and unique nonces; cheap rotation and crypto-shredding.
3. TLS 1.3 everywhere: forward secrecy, AEAD only, HSTS, mTLS internally.
4. Secrets in a manager or replaced by workload identity, scanned, rotated, never logged.

**Follow-ups to expect:** "What happens if you reuse a GCM nonce?"; "How do you rotate a JWT signing key or a database password with zero downtime?"; "A secret was pushed to a public repo ten minutes ago, what do you do?"; "Why not call KMS to encrypt every row?"
keyPoints: Hash to fingerprint, password-hash to store passwords, MAC for shared-key integrity, sign for public verification, AEAD to encrypt.
Use AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 and never reuse a nonce with the same key; bind context with associated data.
Envelope encryption: a KMS-held KEK wraps per-tenant DEKs, making rotation cheap and enabling crypto-shredding.
TLS 1.3 gives one-round-trip handshakes, mandatory forward secrecy and AEAD-only suites; 0-RTT data can be replayed.
Keep secrets in a manager or replace them with workload identity; scan pushes and rotate anything ever committed.
interview: Explain the difference between hashing, encryption, MACs and digital signatures, with a use case for each.
What is envelope encryption and why do systems use a KMS instead of keeping keys in the app?
How do you manage application secrets, and what do you do if a secret is leaked to a public repository?

check.q: Your server must prove to a partner that webhook payloads came from you, and you share a secret with that partner. Which primitive fits best?
options: HMAC-SHA256 of the timestamp and raw body
Base64 encoding with a secret prefix
check.why: A plain hash can be recomputed by anyone. An HMAC requires the shared key, giving integrity and authenticity; the timestamp blocks replays.

check.q: Why do systems encrypt data with a local data key rather than sending every record to KMS?
options: Local keys are stronger than KMS keys
KMS calls are network round trips with quotas and small payload limits; KMS only needs to wrap the data keys
check.why: Envelope encryption keeps bulk crypto local and fast, while the master key stays in KMS and only wraps small DEKs, which also makes rotation cheap.

check.q: Which TLS 1.3 feature needs care because its data can be replayed by an attacker?
check.why: 0-RTT data is sent before the handshake completes and is not protected against replay, so it should only be accepted for idempotent requests.

lessons.summary: A layered request pipeline for secure APIs: schema validation, token-bucket rate limits, correct CORS, security headers, audit logging, and the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023).
lessons.body:
## The core idea

An API is an attack surface that never sleeps: every endpoint, parameter and header is reachable by anyone who can send HTTP, with no UI in the way. API security is the discipline of making each request prove four things before it does work: **who** is calling (authentication), **whether** they may do this to this object (authorization), **that the input is well-formed and bounded** (validation and limits), and **that you will know about it later** (audit logging). On top sit browser-specific controls (CORS, security headers) that only matter because browsers run untrusted code next to your users' cookies.

The OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023 edition) is the best map of where APIs actually break:

| # | Risk | One-line example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| API1 | Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) | `GET /orders/981` returns another user's order |
| API2 | Broken Authentication | No rate limit on `/login`, tokens never expire, weak reset flow |
| API3 | Broken Object Property Level Authorization | Response leaks `passwordHash`; `PATCH /me` accepts `isAdmin` (mass assignment) |
| API4 | Unrestricted Resource Consumption | `?limit=1000000`, 50 MB uploads, a GraphQL query nested 30 levels deep |
| API5 | Broken Function Level Authorization | Any user can call `DELETE /admin/users/42` |
| API6 | Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows | Bots buy all concert tickets or farm sign-up bonuses |
| API7 | Server Side Request Forgery | `POST /webhooks {url: "http://169.254.169.254/..."}` |
| API8 | Security Misconfiguration | Permissive CORS, verbose errors, missing TLS |
| API9 | Improper Inventory Management | Forgotten `/v1` or staging API without the new auth checks |
| API10 | Unsafe Consumption of APIs | Trusting data from a third-party API without validation |

Note that three of the ten are authorization (objects, properties, functions). If you remember one thing: **authorization bugs are the most common serious API bugs**.

## A request pipeline that bakes this in

```text
request
  -> TLS termination, size limit (body <= 1 MB), timeout
  -> rate limiter (per IP, per API key / user, per route cost)
  -> authentication (session cookie or bearer token -> principal)
  -> CSRF / origin check for cookie-authenticated unsafe methods
  -> input validation (schema: types, lengths, enums, unknown keys rejected)
  -> authorization (function level: can call this route? object level: can touch this id?)
  -> handler (parameterised queries, explicit field allowlists)
  -> response shaping (DTO / serializer: only allowed fields)
  -> audit log for security-relevant actions; metrics; generic errors to client
```

Order matters: cheap checks (size, rate) before expensive ones (DB lookups, password hashing).

## Input validation

Validate at the boundary with a schema, and **reject** what does not match rather than trying to clean it. Schema validation stops type confusion (NoSQL operator injection), mass assignment (unknown keys), oversized values and nonsense enums in one place.

```ts
import { z } from "zod";

const UpdateProfile = z
  .object({
    displayName: z.string().trim().min(1).max(80),
    bio: z.string().max(500).optional(),
    website: z.string().url().startsWith("https://").optional(),
    timezone: z.enum(["UTC", "Europe/London", "Asia/Kolkata"]),
  })
  .strict();                                   // unknown keys such as "role" or "isAdmin" are rejected

app.patch("/api/me", requireAuth, async (req, res) => {
  const parsed = UpdateProfile.safeParse(req.body);
  if (!parsed.success) return res.status(400).json({ error: "invalid_input", issues: parsed.error.issues });
  const user = await users.update(req.user.id, parsed.data);   // only validated fields reach the DB
  res.json(toPublicUser(user));                                 // explicit output DTO
});
```

Points interviewers like:

- Validation is about **shape**; it is not a substitute for output encoding (XSS), parameterised queries (SQLi) or authorization.
- Validate on the server even if the client validates; the client is just a convenience.
- Bound everything: string lengths, array sizes, page sizes, numeric ranges, nesting depth, file types (check magic bytes, not just the extension) and file sizes.
- Shape **outputs** too: serialise through an explicit DTO so a new column such as `passwordHash` or `internalNotes` never leaks by default (API3).

## Rate limiting and resource limits

Rate limits protect availability, slow brute force, and contain cost (including LLM calls). Common algorithms:

- **Fixed window**: count per minute; simple, bursts at window edges.
- **Sliding window log or counter**: smoother, a bit more state.
- **Token bucket**: a bucket of capacity B refills at rate R; each request takes a token. Allows short bursts while enforcing an average. Used widely (for example by AWS API Gateway and Stripe's limiters).

```ts
// token bucket in Redis, atomic via a Lua script (sketch)
const script = `
local tokens = tonumber(redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 't') or ARGV[1])
local ts = tonumber(redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 'ts') or ARGV[3])
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])
tokens = math.min(tonumber(ARGV[1]), tokens + (now - ts) * tonumber(ARGV[2]))
local allowed = tokens >= 1
if allowed then tokens = tokens - 1 end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 't', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], 3600)
return allowed and 1 or 0`;
// args: capacity, refill per second, now in seconds; key = `rl:${userId}:${route}`
```

Design choices: limit by **several keys** (IP, user, API key, tenant), weight expensive routes higher, return `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After`, and publish limits in headers (the IETF RateLimit header fields draft is converging on `RateLimit` and `RateLimit-Policy`). Fail open or closed deliberately when the limiter store is down: failing open preserves availability; failing closed protects sensitive endpoints like login.

Beyond request rate: cap page size, request body size, upload size, query complexity (GraphQL depth and cost analysis), regex input length (ReDoS), and per-request timeouts. API6 (business flows) needs product-level limits too: one promo code per account, purchase velocity checks, bot detection.

## CORS: what it is and is not

The **same-origin policy** stops a script on `evil.com` from reading responses from `api.bank.com`. **CORS relaxes that policy**; it does not add protection to your server. A CORS misconfiguration therefore opens a hole; a correct configuration does not stop a server-side attacker, curl or a CSRF form post.

How it works:

- "Simple" requests (GET/POST with simple headers and form content types) are sent directly; the browser then decides whether the page may **read** the response based on `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`.
- Other requests (JSON content type, custom headers, PUT/DELETE) trigger a **preflight** `OPTIONS` request; the browser only sends the real request if the server approves the method, headers and origin.
- With `credentials: "include"`, the server must return the exact origin (not `*`) and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`.

The dangerous pattern is reflecting any `Origin` header back with credentials allowed: any website can then read authenticated responses from your API. Also watch regex allowlists like `/example\.com$/`, which match `evilexample.com`, and allowing the `null` origin (sandboxed iframes can send it).

```ts
const ALLOWED = new Set(["https://app.example.com", "https://admin.example.com"]);

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  const origin = req.get("origin");
  if (origin && ALLOWED.has(origin)) {
    res.set("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", origin);
    res.set("Access-Control-Allow-Credentials", "true");
    res.set("Vary", "Origin");                    // caches must key on Origin
  }
  if (req.method === "OPTIONS") {
    res.set("Access-Control-Allow-Methods", "GET,POST,PATCH,DELETE");
    res.set("Access-Control-Allow-Headers", "Content-Type, Authorization, X-CSRF-Token");
    res.set("Access-Control-Max-Age", "600");
    return res.sendStatus(204);
  }
  next();
});
```

## Security headers

For APIs and the HTML pages that call them, the OWASP HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet and MDN are the references:

| Header | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` | Force HTTPS for a year |
| `Content-Security-Policy` | Restrict script, style, frame and connect sources; a nonce-based `script-src` with `strict-dynamic` is the strongest XSS mitigation; `frame-ancestors 'none'` stops clickjacking |
| `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` | Stop MIME sniffing (a JSON response treated as HTML or script) |
| `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin` | Do not leak full URLs (with tokens or ids) to other sites |
| `Cache-Control: no-store` | For responses with personal data, so shared caches and the back button do not keep them |
| `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy`, `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy` | Isolate your windows and resources from cross-origin pages |

For pure JSON APIs, the essentials are HSTS, `nosniff`, `Cache-Control` on personal data, a restrictive `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'` (cheap insurance) and correct `Content-Type: application/json`.

## Audit logging

Audit logs answer "who did what, to what, when, from where, and was it allowed?" They are different from debug logs: structured, append-only, retained for a defined period, and protected from tampering (write to a separate store or service the application cannot delete from).

```json
{
  "ts": "2026-10-04T06:12:44.120Z",
  "actor": { "type": "user", "id": "u_42", "tenant": "t_acme", "sessionId": "s_hash_9f1" },
  "action": "invoice.approve",
  "target": { "type": "invoice", "id": "inv_981" },
  "result": "allowed",
  "ip": "203.0.113.7",
  "userAgent": "Mozilla/5.0 ...",
  "requestId": "req_7c2e"
}
```

Log: logins (success and failure), MFA changes, password resets, permission and role changes, API key creation, admin actions, data exports, authorization denials. **Never log** passwords, tokens, session ids (log a hash), full card numbers or other secrets; be careful with personal data. Alert on patterns such as bursts of 401/403, an admin logging in from a new country, or mass exports.

## API inventory and versions

API9 is boring and deadly: an old `/v1` endpoint without the new authorization middleware, a staging host with production data, or a debug route left in. Keep an inventory (an OpenAPI spec generated from code), route every version through the same auth middleware, retire versions on a schedule, and scan for undocumented endpoints.

## Common mistakes

- Relying on CORS to "secure" an API.
- Returning ORM objects directly as JSON.
- Rate limiting only by IP, or not at all on login, OTP and password-reset routes.
- `limit` and `offset` parameters with no maximum.
- Verbose error responses with stack traces and SQL.
- API keys in query strings (they end up in logs and `Referer` headers); send them in headers.
- Treating third-party API responses as trusted (API10): validate them like user input.

## In the interview

**What they probe:** a layered mental model, BOLA as the top risk, practical rate limiting, an accurate understanding of CORS, and operational maturity (audit logs, inventory).

**A 60-second answer outline:**
1. Pipeline: size and rate limits, authentication, CSRF check for cookies, schema validation with unknown keys rejected, function- and object-level authorization, explicit output DTOs.
2. Token-bucket rate limiting keyed by user, IP and route cost, returning 429 with `Retry-After`.
3. CORS is an allowlist that relaxes the same-origin policy; never reflect arbitrary origins with credentials.
4. Security headers (HSTS, CSP, nosniff, no-store) and structured, tamper-resistant audit logs.
5. Map to the OWASP API Top 10, especially BOLA and property-level authorization.

**Follow-ups to expect:** "Design rate limiting for a public API with free and paid tiers"; "Why does a preflight happen and what does it check?"; "What would you put in an audit log, and what would you keep out?"; "How do you stop mass assignment?"
keyPoints: Three of the OWASP API Top 10 are authorization failures: object level (BOLA), property level and function level.
Validate inputs with strict schemas that reject unknown keys, bound every size, and serialise outputs through explicit DTOs.
Rate limit with a token bucket keyed by user, IP and route cost; return 429 with Retry-After.
CORS relaxes the same-origin policy; it never protects the server, and reflecting any Origin with credentials is a hole.
Audit logs record actor, action, target, result and request id in a tamper-resistant store, without secrets.

check.q: An API sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin to whatever Origin header it receives and also sends Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. What is the impact?
options: None, because CORS is enforced by the server
Any website a logged-in user visits can read authenticated API responses
check.why: The browser trusts the reflected origin and allows the page to read responses sent with the user's cookies, exposing their data to any site.

check.q: PATCH /api/me binds the whole JSON body into the user model, and an attacker sends {"role": "admin"}. Which OWASP API risk is this?
options: API3 Broken Object Property Level Authorization (mass assignment)
check.why: The caller may update their own object but not that property. A strict schema or explicit field allowlist prevents it.

check.q: Why is a token bucket a popular rate-limiting algorithm for APIs?
options: It allows short bursts up to the bucket size while enforcing a long-run average rate
It needs no state at all
It guarantees exactly one request per second
It blocks all requests from new IP addresses
check.why: Tokens refill at rate R up to capacity B, so clients can burst briefly but cannot exceed the average, which matches real client behaviour.

projects.title: Production-grade auth service with sessions, OIDC, passkeys and fine-grained authorization
projects.summary: A self-hosted identity service for a multi-tenant SaaS: password, passkey and TOTP login, server sessions, an OIDC server (code + PKCE, client credentials) with rotating refresh tokens and JWKS key rotation, relationship-based permissions and a tamper-evident audit log.
projects.why: Auth is where interviewers separate people who used a library from people who understand the threats. This project lets you defend every decision with specifics: why Argon2id parameters, why refresh token reuse revokes a family, how keys rotate without downtime, how a cross-tenant request is blocked twice (application and RLS), and how you tested it with an attack suite. It maps directly onto backend and security interview questions.
projects.architecture:
```text
browser (demo SaaS) --cookie __Host-sid--> BFF / app server --> resource API (verifies JWT via JWKS)
        |                                        |                       |
        |  login, passkeys, TOTP                 | OIDC code + PKCE      | authz.check(user, action, obj)
        v                                        v                       v
   +-------------------- auth service (Fastify) ----------------------+
   | /login /webauthn/* /mfa/*  /authorize /token /jwks.json /userinfo |
   | /.well-known/openid-configuration  /revoke  /introspect           |
   | rate limiter (Redis token bucket, Postgres fallback)              |
   | key manager: active + previous signing keys (kid), KMS-wrapped     |
   +--------------------------------------------------------------------+
        | Postgres: users, credentials, sessions(hash), refresh_tokens(family),
        |           clients, relation_tuples, audit_log (hash chain), RLS by tenant
```
Key decisions: server sessions for the first-party app and JWT access tokens only for APIs; Argon2id with rehash-on-login; refresh tokens opaque, hashed and rotated with family revocation; ES256 signing keys with kid-based rotation and private keys wrapped by a KMS (or a local master key in dev); a Zanzibar-style tuple table for sharing plus RBAC for admin; tenant isolation enforced in repositories and by Postgres RLS.

deepDives.title: Refresh token rotation with reuse detection
deepDives.body:
Refresh tokens are 256-bit random strings returned once and stored only as SHA-256 hashes in a `refresh_tokens` table with `family_id`, `parent_id`, `used_at`, `expires_at` and `family_expires_at`.

```text
refresh(rt):
  row = find by hash(rt)
  if !row or expired -> invalid_grant
  if row.used_at != null:
      if now - row.used_at < 5s and same client -> return the child already issued (tab race)
      else revoke all rows in row.family_id; audit 'refresh_reuse'; invalid_grant
  mark row used; insert child with same family; issue new access token
```

The whole operation runs in one transaction with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the row so two concurrent refreshes cannot both succeed. The short grace window handles two browser tabs refreshing at once without logging the user out; outside it, reuse is treated as theft. The family has an absolute lifetime (for example 30 days) so a continuously rotated chain still ends. Trade-off: the grace window slightly weakens detection, so it is limited to the same client id and a few seconds.

deepDives.title: Zero-downtime signing key rotation
deepDives.body:
Signing keys live in a `signing_keys` table with states `next`, `active`, `retiring` and `retired`; private keys are stored wrapped by a KMS key (or a local master key in development).

```text
day 0   publish K2 as next in JWKS (K1 active)        verifiers cache both
day 1   switch: K2 active, K1 retiring             new tokens kid=K2, old kid=K1 still verify
day 1 + max token lifetime  remove K1 from JWKS
```

Publishing the next key before using it matters because verifiers cache the JWKS; `jose`'s remote JWKS refetches on unknown `kid`, but other clients may cache for hours. The rotation job is idempotent and audited. An emergency rotation (suspected key leak) skips the waiting period, removes the old key immediately and accepts that outstanding tokens fail, which forces re-authentication via refresh tokens.

deepDives.title: Two layers of tenant isolation
Passkeys and account recovery
deepDives.body:
Passkey registration stores the credential id, public key, sign counter, transports and a user-chosen label. Login uses discoverable credentials with conditional UI (autofill), verifying the challenge (single use, 5-minute expiry), origin, rpId hash and user verification flag.

Recovery is the weak point of any strong-auth system. The design: users must have at least two authenticators or recovery codes before passwords can be removed; recovery codes are hashed and single-use; using one forces enrolment of a new passkey and notifies the user by email; changing MFA settings requires a fresh authentication within 5 minutes and triggers a 24-hour notification window. Support-assisted recovery is out of scope for the demo but documented as the main residual risk.
